notes.meaning: Paul is shocked that believers would drag each other into secular courts to settle private disputes. The word unrighteous does not mean pagan judges were always crooked, but that they did not know the true God. True believers, who are called saints or God's holy people, should be able to resolve their differences with each other in love. Christians should never bring public shame on the gospel by fighting in front of the world.

Paul reminds the church that believers will share with Christ in the final judgment of the world. Because God has chosen His people for such a great future honor, they should easily be able to handle small earthly disagreements. Earthly property and everyday quarrels are very small matters compared to eternity.

Believers will even take part in approving the judgment of rebellious, evil angels on the last day. If Christians will evaluate spiritual powers, they certainly have enough understanding through God's truth to settle everyday business matters. We must remember our high calling in Christ when we are tempted to quarrel.

Paul asks why they choose judges who have no standing in the church when they need to settle daily matters. Some read this as a sharp question rebuking them for turning to pagans, while others see it as advice to pick even the lowliest church member over an outside judge. Either way, believers ought not to hand over church disputes to the secular world.

Paul speaks this directly to their shame to puncture their boastful pride. The Corinthians loved to brag about their wisdom, yet their actions showed they could not find a single wise person among them to help two brothers settle an argument. God wants His people to use practical wisdom and peacemaking within the church family.

Instead of making peace, Christian brothers were hauling one another before heathen courts. This made the church look foolish and unloving in front of unbelievers who watched their selfish fighting. When we harbor bitter disputes, we harm the witness of Jesus before a watching world.

Paul declares that the very existence of lawsuits among them means they have already lost the battle. Even if a person wins a legal case, Christian love and fellowship have suffered a terrible defeat. It is far better to be wronged or cheated out of money than to damage the honor of Jesus.

Instead of patiently enduring an injury, the Corinthians were actually the ones cheating and hurting others. To make matters worse, they were doing this to their own brothers and sisters in Christ. Those who belong to God should show fairness and family love, never dishonesty.

Paul warns that anyone who lives an unrepentant life of wrongdoing will not inherit God's kingdom. He lists several kinds of willful sin, including idolatry, sexual sins between men, theft, drunkenness, greed, and slander. Paul is not talking about someone who struggles and repents, but about people whose lives are defined by continuous rebellion against God.

Paul reminds them that some in the church used to live in those exact sins, but God completely changed them. They were washed clean from their past guilt, set apart to be holy, and justified, which means declared righteous before God through Jesus and the Holy Spirit. No matter how broken our past was, God's grace gives us a clean slate and power to live purely.

differ.view: Sanctification follows as a fruit of justification, where a believer is pardoned first through Christ's merits and then inwardly made holy by the Spirit.
Justification and sanctification are distinct gifts that always go together in conversion, cleansing both the legal guilt and the inward pollution of sin.

notes.meaning: Some Corinthians used the slogan that everything is permissible to justify their selfish desires and questionable habits. Paul replies that even when something is not strictly forbidden, it may not be helpful or good for others. Furthermore, a Christian must never allow any appetite or habit to become a master over their life. True freedom in Christ means having the power to say no to harmful things.

The Corinthians excused their sexual desires by comparing them to eating food, saying God made the stomach for food. Paul explains that while physical food and the stomach only last for this temporary life, the human body has an eternal purpose for the Lord. Our bodies were never created for sexual immorality, but to serve Christ and belong to Him.

God raised Jesus from the dead by His mighty power, and He will raise believers up with new bodies in the same way. Because our bodies will be raised to live forever in holiness, they are sacred and important to God. Knowing that our bodies belong to eternity should keep us from degrading them with sin.

Paul asks if they realize that their physical bodies are joined to Christ as parts of His own spiritual body. The idea of taking what belongs to Jesus and uniting it with a prostitute is completely shocking and unthinkable. Christians must treat their bodies with reverence because they are bound to a holy Savior.

Paul explains from Scripture that physical intimacy creates a real one flesh bond between two people, quoting Genesis about marriage. When someone joins with a prostitute, that sacred union is dragged into corruption and shame. There is no such thing as meaningless casual sex in God's eyes, because it deeply joins two lives together.

In contrast to physical impurity, anyone who is united to the Lord becomes one with Him in spirit. This close, holy relationship fills the human heart with true life and peace. A person who enjoys this spiritual bond with Christ should never trade it for sinful pleasures.

Paul gives a direct command to run away from sexual immorality immediately. Other sins happen outside the body, but sexual sin uniquely damages and stains a person's own body and purpose. The only safe way to defeat sexual temptation is not to debate it, but to flee from it on the spot.

Paul reminds every believer that their physical body is a holy temple where the Holy Spirit lives. God gave this Spirit to dwell inside each Christian, which means believers no longer own themselves. We do not have the right to use our bodies however we please, because they belong to God.

Christians belong to God because Jesus paid for them with His own precious blood on the cross. Since God paid such a high price to rescue us, we are called to honor and praise Him with our physical bodies. Everything we do with our bodies should reflect the goodness and glory of our Lord.
